title: Vortex matter as a magnetically programmable metasurface for tuning near-field radiative heat transfer
summary: Near-field radiative heat transfer (NFRHT) is of great interest for energy conversion and thermal management. Recent work on NFRHT has shown that metasurfaces can enhance NFRHT and reshape its spectral characteristics. Here, we show that the vortex lattice of a type-II superconductor represents a self-assembled metasurface whose lattice dimensions, in contrast to most other metasurfaces, can be tuned by magnetic fields, allowing NFRHT to be varied by orders of magnitude. Specifically, we show that for two Nb surfaces at 4.2 K and separated by a 100 nm gap, NFRHT can be magnetically tuned by a factor >200. Further, we show that the tuning range grows upon cooling, exceeding 10^5 at 2 K, which is far beyond the order-unity modulation of many proposed schemes for tuning NFRHT. Our results establish vortex matter as a magnetically programmable thermal metasurface and open new opportunities for tuning the flow of heat at the nanoscale.

title: High-Field and Light-Dependent Magnetization Provides Evidence for Coexisting Granular Superconductivity and Superparamagnetism in Nitrogen-Doped Diamond
summary: We investigated the field-, temperature-, and time-dependent magnetic moment of a nitrogen-doped type Ib diamond in darkness and under monochromatic light with a low laser intensity of about 160 $μ$W cm$^{-2}$. In darkness, below approximately 25 K, the magnetic moment exhibits unconventional hysteresis loops that can be explained by the coexistence of superparamagnetism and superconductivity in certain regions of the sample. Under illumination, this hysteresis largely disappears, leaving mainly the superparamagnetic contribution. Temperature-dependent measurements reveal an irreversibility below 25 K in darkness, which vanishes under illumination. Similarly, at 0.5 T and below 25 K, the time-dependent magnetization shows flux-creep-like behavior that disappears when the sample is illuminated. All light-induced changes are fully reversible: the magnetic properties measured in darkness are restored after the sample is heated above roughly 50 K. Removing the superparamagnetic contribution from magnetization measurements up to $\pm 14$ T reveals clear characteristics of a granular superconductor, namely, a well-defined penetration field $H_p \approx 2.6$ T and a critical field $H_{c2} \approx 10.6$ T. Based on theoretical considerations, we attribute the observed phenomena to the combined effects of internal stress and local variations in nitrogen concentration within localized regions that can be regarded as grains. This interpretation is supported by Raman and birefringence spectroscopy measurements on the same sample.

title: Rashba-controlled emergence and reversal of critical-field anisotropy in p-wave magnet--superconductor hybrids
comment: 14 pages, 10 figures. Submitted to Physical Review B on October 6, 2026
summary: We show that tuning Rashba spin-orbit coupling can change the in-plane field direction along which an $s$-wave superconductor is most susceptible to Zeeman depairing. We consider a two-dimensional $s$-wave superconductor subject to an odd-parity exchange field induced by a $p$-wave magnet. Without Rashba coupling, the out-of-plane exchange field enhances the in-plane critical field but leaves its angular response exactly isotropic, despite the anisotropic magnetic spin texture. Minimizing the Bogoliubov--de Gennes grand potential over uniform singlet pairing, we find that increasing Rashba coupling first generates and then reverses the principal-axis critical-field contrast, switching the minimum-critical-field direction by $90^{\circ}$. Equal principal-axis fields at the intervening compensation point coexist with residual angular modulation. We interpret the reversal through competing momentum-dependent depairing contributions from the magnetic and Rashba spin textures, while the on-site singlet pairing channel remains unchanged. Direction-dependent discontinuous collapses of the order parameter further shape the critical-field curves. These results identify a tunable directional paramagnetic response within the uniform-pairing sector. In heterostructures with sufficient electrostatic tunability of interfacial Rashba coupling, this reversal would enable gate control of the easy-depairing axis without reorienting the magnetic texture.

title: Pressure-induced superconductivity in a bilayer metal
summary: We propose a model that explains the mechanism of pressure-induced superconductivity in a bilayer metal. Four types of pair potentials are assumed for a Cooper pair consisting of two electrons on different layers. Absence of local inversion symmetry gives rise to the spin-orbit coupling which is antisymmetric in the two layers. We assume that external pressure enhances the hybridization between the two layers. The stability of the superconducting states is well explained by the frequency symmetry of the induced pairing correlations by these potentials. Pressure-induced superconductivity emerges when the following two conditions are realized. (i) The spin-orbit coupling induces the odd-frequency pairing correlations and suppresses superconductivity at ambient pressure. (ii) The interplay between the spin-orbit coupling and the hybridization induces the additional pairing correlation that belongs to an even-frequency symmetry class. We briefly discuss the relevance of our model to real materials.

title: Zeeman Quantum Geometry of the Layer Pseudo-spin
summary: Two-dimensional layers coupled by position-dependent interlayer tunnelling host a layer pseudo-spin whose polarization is a controllable internal degree of freedom. We introduce the quantum geometry of this layer pseudo-spin: a mixed tensor formed from the interband Berry connection and the layer matrix element, which governs the response to an oscillating in-plane electric field. Because the layer pseudo-spin is an Ising-type scalar invariant under threefold rotation, its selection rules differ from those of a pseudovector spin. In a minimal two-band model, the layer-pseudo-spin quantum metric and Zeeman--Berry curvature are nonzero, while their zone integrals vanish. An in-plane drive therefore leaves the spatially averaged polarization unchanged at linear order but imprints a moiré-periodic intracell pattern, directly imageable by layer-resolved tunnelling. For twisted MoTe$_2$ bilayer, we quantify the local dipole modulation and identify the rectified, helicity-odd, and third-harmonic channels through which a net response appears at higher order.

title: Andreev Scattering Driven Surface Photogalvanic Effect
summary: The surface photogalvanic effect is a powerful tool for generating macroscopic direct currents in centrosymmetric film structures via asymmetric scattering of carriers at film boundaries. Here, we uncover a fundamentally distinct regime of photoinduced transport in normal metal-superconductor heterostructures, in which the macroscopic photocurrent is governed by Andreev scattering at the interface rather than by classical scattering. We demonstrate that the interplay between asymmetric surface scattering and Andreev retroreflection yields a giant, strongly frequency-dependent anomalous photocurrent. Strikingly, the electron-hole conversion at the normal-superconducting interface dictates a macroscopic sign reversal of the photogalvanic current across the superconducting transition, and induces non-analytic spectral kinks exactly at the pairing gap frequency. Our results establish the Andreev reflection-driven surface photogalvanic effect as a platform for optical control of superconducting correlations and suggest a direct, non-invasive spectroscopic probe for gap dynamics in hybrid quantum devices.

title: Stacking-Induced Tuning of a Flat-Band Surface State in NbIrTe4
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to Phys. Rev. B
summary: Ternary layered transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) offer high tunability and access to correlated and topological states. However, like the broader family of layered TMDCs, their properties are sensitive to stacking order and interlayer coupling. Here, we investigate the electronic structure and surface states of NbIrTe$_4$, a candidate Weyl semimetal in bulk, and predicted to be a quantum spin Hall insulator in monolayer form. Using scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM), angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), and density-functional theory (DFT), we attribute the strong resonance in tunnelling spectroscopy located approximately 8 meV below the Fermi level to a surface-derived flat band which shows sensitivity to the local stacking order at the surface. In regions where the top layer is laterally shifted, tunnelling spectroscopy instead shows a gap-like feature with intensity near the Fermi level shifted in energy. Combining DFT and quasiparticle interference (QPI) measurements, we find this dramatic change in the spectroscopy in the vicinity of the quasi-1D flat-band surface state becomes dispersive due to a change in the spatial distribution of the density of states in the top two layers. These findings establish NbIrTe$_4$ as a platform where surface band dispersion can be effectively tuned through local structural manipulation.

title: Non-uniform grids to accelerate electron-phonon coupling calculations for superconductivity
summary: Efficient and accurate evaluation of electron-phonon interactions is essential for predictive superconductivity calculations, but dense Brillouin zone sampling requirements pose a major computational bottleneck. To overcome this, we introduce an accelerated, highly scalable framework that combines a double delta truncation scheme with non-uniform Farey grids in both $\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ space. The truncation strategy significantly reduces computational cost by restricting integration to states satisfying energy constraints near the Fermi level, while the Farey grids dynamically resolve sampling errors from localized scattering and stabilize convergence. Applied to elemental aluminium and several high-pressure hydrides, this combined methodology reduces computational cost by up to two orders of magnitude and yields electron-phonon coupling constants and superconducting critical temperatures Tc typically within about 5% of full-grid benchmarks. This approach overcomes sampling bottlenecks associated with dense uniform grids, making accurate, low-cost predictions of superconductivity in complex quantum materials feasible.

title: Quantum Oscillations across Hole Crystallization in Rhombohedral Graphene
summary: Recent quantum-oscillation measurements in rhombohedral graphene reveal an abrupt increase in the dominant frequency and the emergence of additional frequencies as the carrier density is lowered toward superconductivity. Noninteracting band models can account for multiple frequencies but do not explain the upward jump. We show that these features can arise from two competing fates of the inner hole pocket in an annular Fermi sea: collapse into a simply connected Fermi liquid or crystallization into an anticrystal, in which localized holes coexist with itinerant electrons. Pocket collapse contracts the outer Fermi contour at fixed density, whereas hole crystallization preserves a larger contour that supports magnetic-breakdown orbits. This contrast provides a possible explanation for the frequency jump, while additional reconstructed orbits produce a multitone spectrum. Our results support the anticrystal as a candidate normal state near superconductivity in rhombohedral graphene.

title: Superconducting weak links at substrate steps in bilayer nickelate films
summary: Ambient-pressure superconductivity above 40 K has been realized in bilayer nickelate thin films on SrLaAlO$_4$ (001), yet resistive measurements often exhibit incomplete zero-resistance states and/or two-step superconducting transitions of unresolved origin. We show that these features arise from superconducting weak links at substrate step-terrace structures. A direct correlation between the azimuthal-angle-dependent two-step transition and step-terrace orientation establishes this connection, further supported by atomic-scale visualization of structurally disrupted regions at step terraces. Modeling the films as pristine (weak-link) regions with higher (lower) transition temperature reproduces essential features of the two-step transition using both a simple model and finite-element simulations. Transport measurements further reveal a strong dependence of transition characteristics - and even the occurrence of superconductivity itself - on average terrace width. These results identify step-induced weak links as the microscopic origin of two-step transitions in bilayer nickelate films, providing a framework for understanding anisotropic and percolative transport, and a route to superconducting devices.

title: Ballistic transport and crystallographic control in altermagnetic quantum rings
summary: We study coherent two-terminal transport through a finite-width $d$-wave altermagnetic quantum ring with nonmagnetic leads. A confined Aharonov--Bohm flux remains exactly $h/e$ periodic and, in the symmetric one-mode geometry, produces an exact half-flux transmission zero. A perpendicular field shifts the interference pattern according to an effective area $A_{\rm eff}=1.0342\,πr_0^2$ and the altermagnetic splitting resolves the common zero into nearby spin-dependent nodes. Rotating the crystal reverses the transmitted spin, whereas the mirror orientation $θ_A=π/4$ is exactly spin degenerate. For a $50$~nm reference ring, sub-tesla fields yield windows with $|P_T|>0.99$, the most accessible of which requires a uniform field alone and no confined flux. Finite-bias, thermal, disorder, Zeeman, and spin-conserving voltage-probe calculations show that the polarization is appreciably more stable than individual coherent-resonance amplitudes. These results identify interference-node positions, flux periodicity, and crystal-controlled spin polarization as experimentally useful signatures of an altermagnetic mesoscopic interferometer.

title: Saturating $T^2$ resistivity in iron-based superconductors
summary: Many correlated metals exhibit a crossover from low-temperature $ρ\propto T^{2}$ behavior to a slower increase of the resistivity at elevated temperatures. Distinguishing phonon scattering from electron--electron correlations as the origin of this crossover is experimentally challenging. We introduce a simple phenomenological framework that isolates the contribution responsible for the high-temperature saturating tendency. This approach reveals a clear contrast between systems well known for the predominance of electron--phonon scattering and several iron-based superconductors. For the latter, the conductivity can be expressed as the sum of a Fermi-liquid-like term ($\propto 1/T^{2}$) and a temperature-independent component, which together describe $ρ(T)$ up to $\sim 250$ K in LiFeAs, KFe$_2$As$_2$, and KCaFe$_4$As$_4$. In FeSe, the same approach identifies a similar regime above the nematic transition, with a pronounced change toward nearly linear-in-$T$ resistivity below it. We discuss these findings in the broader context of coherence and electronic correlations in Hund's metals.

title: Diffusive Description of Superconducting Single-Photon Detectors Using Quantum Mechanics
summary: The methodology of non-Hermitian quantum mechanics is employed to parameterize the dynamics of coupled classical diffusion equations describing low- and high-energy quasiparticles in superconducting single-photon detectors in one to three spatial dimensions.

title: Steering of topological criticality in the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain via non-Hermitian substitutional impurities
summary: We investigate the topological phase in a one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain in the presence of a finite concentration of non-Hermitian substitutional impurities. Our primary focus is the discovery of a deterministic mechanism to actively reconfigure the topological phase boundaries by introducing site-dependent, non-reciprocal intracell and intercell hopping amplitudes. Specifically, breaking the internal structural symmetry of the non-reciprocal impurity hoppings induces a targeted macroscopic displacement of the critical point. This mechanism allows for the controlled expansion or compression of the topological phase strictly via local defect asymmetry. We validate this boundary displacement through finite-size scaling analysis. The extracted correlation length critical exponents ($ν\approx 1.455$ and $ν\approx 1.397$ for symmetric and asymmetric configurations, respectively) confirm a disorder-induced departure from the pristine SSH universality class, with the exponent diverging at high defect densities. We also report an impurity-induced real-to-complex spectral transition geometrically characterized by the Non-Hermitian Skin Effect. Ultimately, our results establish how isolated non-Hermitian asymmetries cooperatively interact to deterministically shift macroscopic topological protection.

title: Magnetic-Field-Induced Darkening of Bright Excitons in a MoWSe$_2$ Monolayer Alloy
summary: Magnetic fields are widely used to brighten spin-forbidden dark excitons, but the inverse effect on an optically bright exciton has remained largely unexplored. We demonstrate the complementary phenomenon of magnetic-field-induced darkening of a bright exciton in Mo$_{0.68}$W$_{0.32}$Se$_2$. At 4.2 K, an in-plane magnetic field up to 25 T activates a dark-exciton line 14.2$\pm$1.3 meV below the bright exciton while suppressing the bright-exciton emission by about 85\%. A bright-dark mixing model quantitatively captures the coupled energy and intensity evolution with an effective in-plane $g$ factor of $|g_{\parallel}|=5.2\pm0.2$. Alloying is crucial to the effect, as it brings the system close to the bright-dark crossover, where a small bright-dark splitting is combined with unusually strong in-plane magnetic coupling. This places the system in a regime where field-induced level repulsion raises the bright-like branch and strongly depletes its thermal population. These results identify a general route to magnetic control of exciton populations through engineering of the bright-dark hierarchy.

title: Magnetic-Field Effects on the Electronic States of the K$_4$ Lattice
summary: We investigate the electronic states of the K$_4$ lattice in a uniform magnetic field within a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. The K$_4$ lattice is a \rev{noncentrosymmetric three-dimensional network with triple-Dirac cones at the $Γ$ and H points}. By fixing the Bloch momentum component parallel to the field, the Peierls-substituted tight-binding problem reduces to an effective two-dimensional problem and yields a Hofstadter spectrum \rev{whose self-similar subpatterns reflect the geometry of the lattice projected onto the plane perpendicular to the field}. A square-like substructure emerges on the flux scale $φ= 1/8$ for $\bm{B}\parallel[100]$, and honeycomb- and triangular-like substructures emerge on the finer scale $φ= 1/32$ for $\bm{B}\parallel[111]$\rev{. Here $φ$ is the flux through the elementary plaquette of the projected lattice, and these scales correspond to one flux quantum per projected unit cell. Owing to the screw axes of the chiral K$_4$ network, the field-parallel momentum acts as an additional flux, which, for commensurate values of this momentum, shifts the spectrum along the flux axis and brings the second triple-Dirac cone at the H point into the magnetic spectrum}. In the weak-field limit, we derive the Landau-level structure from a low-energy effective Hamiltonian around the $Γ$ point. The three-component nature of the triple-Dirac cone gives rise to a cubic secular equation, whose solutions describe how a pseudospin-flat branch coexists with two relativistic Landau ladders \rev{and a single chiral $n=0$ level dispersing linearly along the field, in agreement with the lattice calculation}.

title: Collective Hall quantization in 3D Chern vector systems
comment: This manuscript substantially revises and supersedes our earlier preprint (arXiv:2501.14493), with a restructured presentation and a different scientific emphasis
summary: Understanding the three-dimensional (3D) quantum Hall effect, characterized by a Chern vector rather than a single Chern number, has been a central pursuit in topological physics. While quantized Hall transport is established for the special case with one nonzero Chern component, recent realizations of more general Chern-vector states raise a fundamental question: how does such topology protect quantized transport? Here, we predict a distinct 3D quantized Hall effect protected by $\mathbf{C}=(0,m,n)$. For samples with dimensions $L_y$ and $L_z$, global topology enforces collective quantization of $mL_y+nL_z$, despite the fragility of individual edge modes to disorder. This reveals a novel transport regime in which robust quantization emerges as a holistic property of a unified chiral network,rather than of its constituent modes. Crucially, this collective response manifests as a quantized Hall conductance $G_{xy}=\pm(mL_y+nL_z)e^2/h$, with a distinctive dependence on both Chern-vector components and sample dimensions. We propose candidate materials to facilitate experimental observation.

title: On the origin of nonreciprocal charge transport in topological insulator BiSbTeSe2
summary: Nonreciprocal charge transport provides an effective approach for probing direction dependent charge dynamics and spin-momentum-locked electronic states. Here, we report highly gate-tunable nonreciprocal charge transport in dual-gated BiSbTeSe2 topological insulator device. The second-harmonic longitudinal resistance is linear in both current and magnetic field. The nonreciprocal response reaches its maximum near the charge neutrality point, exhibits sign reversals on either side, and is strongly suppressed once the Fermi level enters the bulk states. We suggest that the nonreciprocal response is attributed to the inhomogeneity of spin-momentum locking in the topological surface states. The nonreciprocal signal near the charge neutrality point is about one order of magnitude larger than that without gate modulation and remains robust up to 300 K, highlighting BiSbTeSe2 as a promising platform for room-temperature nonlinear electronics.

title: Polarity-selective domain wall propagation driven by spin-orbit torque
summary: Spatial variations in magnetic anisotropy impede the spin-orbit-torque-driven motion of chiral domain walls in perpendicularly magnetized nanowires. We show that the local geometry of a two-dimensional anisotropy landscape can select which wall polarity propagates under a given current. Micromagnetic simulations of spatially correlated random anisotropy landscapes generated by diffusion-based smoothing reveal different propagation outcomes for up--down and down--up walls within the same disorder realization. A single inclined anisotropy boundary isolates the mechanism: in the presence of the Dzyaloshinskii--Moriya interaction, opposite wall polarities develop opposite current-induced tilts, producing different alignment with the boundary and hence different pinning strengths. Reversing the boundary inclination interchanges the pinned and propagating polarities. An extended collective-coordinate model captures this geometric selection and distinguishes the propagation threshold from the static pinning limit.

title: Time-Reversal Symmetry in Artificial Topological Graphene Rings
summary: We study an artificial graphene ring described by the low-energy two-valley Dirac Hamiltonian with a uniform mass term. When the ring is threaded by an Aharonov-Bohm flux, the problem reduces to a second-order radial equation solved by Bessel functions. We give the exact secular equation and, for narrow rings, closed expressions for the spectrum and the persistent current. We then add a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane. The radial problem is solved with confluent hypergeometric functions, and the persistent current and magnetization are written as derivatives of a secular determinant from which the spurious roots have been removed. Besides the usual orbital coupling, the field enters through a valley-dependent term that comes from the Dirac structure and lifts the valley degeneracy. A weak-field expansion, accurate up to corrections of order B^4, gives this valley splitting explicitly and separates the diamagnetic and paramagnetic contributions to the susceptibility. Finally, we work out what time reversal implies for the spectrum. Physical time reversal, which exchanges the valleys, leads to an exact relation between levels at opposite fields. The effective single-valley time reversal, on the other hand, is broken by the mass term and by the boundary conditions, yet leaves no trace in the zero-field spectrum. Numerical results for the spectrum, the persistent current, and the magnetization illustrate the analysis.

title: Adiabatic confinement and number-theoretic spectra of massless Dirac fermions in twisted trilayer graphene
summary: Electrons in graphene move like massless relativistic particles, making them exceptionally mobile but difficult to trap because Klein tunnelling permits unimpeded passage through electrostatic barriers. This challenge extends to atomic collapse and hadron confinement. Twisted trilayers form Bernal and rhombohedral domains joined by smooth boundaries, bringing their carriers into contact. Here we show that a new mechanism, distinct from established approaches, confines massless fermions in equilateral triangular Bernal domains without mass barriers, bulk gaps or physical edges. Simulations and analytical modeling reveal that massless carriers have no adiabatic continuation into rhombohedral domains, while escape through nonadiabatic coupling to massive carriers is exponentially suppressed by smooth stacking variation. Perfect reflection in the adiabatic limit turns Bernal domains into quantum cavities in a gapless, edgeless metal. Striking density-of-states oscillations encode Eisenstein-integer arithmetic, linking energies and degeneracies to norms and prime factorizations. These findings bring relativistic confinement and number theory into experimentally accessible electronic spectra.

title: Density Saturation and Autocorrelation Characteristics of Interlayer Exciton Ensembles in MoSe$_2$/WSe$_2$ Heterostructures
summary: We investigate interlayer excitons in MoSe$_2$/WSe$_2$ heterostructures using time-resolved photoluminescence and second-order autocorrelation measurements across a wide range of excitation powers and bath temperatures. By analyzing the photoluminescence amplitude and lifetime of the interlayer exciton state with the lowest emission energy, we extract a corresponding density-temperature diagram. The extracted exciton density exhibits a saturation at approximately $10^{13}$cm$^{-2}$, consistent with values predicted for a Mott transition of interlayer exciton ensembles in van der Waals heterostructures. Moreover, possible interpretations beyond the Mott transition are discussed. We further test whether the density limit is accompanied by a departure from classical photon statistics. The second-order autocorrelation measurements reveal that the photoluminescence maintains an emission characteristic of $g^{(2)}(0) \approx 1$ from low exciton densities up to the maximum reachable density in the investigated exciton ensembles consistent with the lowest-energy exciton ensemble obeying Poissonian statistics.

title: Steady-state cooperative emission of interlayer excitons in atomically thin light-emitting diodes
summary: When an ensemble of emitters is confined within an optical wavelength, its radiation can become correlated, leading to cooperative emission. In two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) electron-hole bilayers, strong light-matter coupling enables the formation of interlayer excitons (IXs), long-lived dipolar excitations that provide an ideal setting for emergent collective phenomena. Here, we engineer an atomically thin light-emitting diode (LED) that generates electroluminescence (EL) from electrically injected IXs that are confined near the sample edges by an edge-enhanced fringing electric field. By measuring Hanbury-Brown-Twiss photon-photon correlations, we find pronounced signatures of collective decay in the form of large photon bunching followed by finite delay antibunching and bunching revivals. These emitter correlation signatures disappear when free charge carriers are doped to form a degenerate Fermi sea but are enhanced by the introduction of localized electrons. The results are consistent with a many-body quantum master equation that models the steady-state superradiant photon statistics of incoherently injected IXs. Our work establishes steady-state cooperative emission in a 2D TMD LED as a platform for studying strong light-matter interactions in electrically driven, non-equilibrium phases of Bose-Fermi mixtures.

title: Electronic driving of torsional modes in carbon nanotubes via orbital-phonon coupling
summary: We theoretically investigate electronic driving of a torsional mode in a suspended carbon nanotube quantum dot. The valley states in a nanotube carry opposite orbital magnetic moments along the tube axis, and intervalley mixing forms valley-mixed eigenstates whose splitting can be controlled by an axial magnetic field. We formulate an orbital-rotation coupling between the torsional angular velocity and the valley orbital angular momentum. Using a master equation for sequential tunneling through normal-metal electrodes, we calculate the steady-state current and the phonon distribution of the torsional mode. When the valley-state splitting matches the torsional phonon energy, orbital transitions can drive the mode out of equilibrium. The contacts control both phonon pumping and its electrical readout, allowing substantial excitation with a positive, vanishing, or negative current response. The mechanism requires no intrinsic spin or valley polarization of the electrodes, but uses state-dependent tunneling at the contacts.

title: Spin-wave circulation in unbounded ferromagnetic film
summary: A key challenge in spin-wave computing is steering spin waves through circuits without wave distortion or reflections. This often results in 1D propagation scenarios, which hinder applicability in 2D magnonic circuits. We demonstrate experimentally a novel approach using a hard magnetic spherical microparticle to guide spin-waves onto a closed path in a plain thin YIG film. The particle stray field induces a radially symmetrical magnetization landscape, which allows spin-waves to loop around. In parallel, we conducted micromagnetic simulations reproducing the experimental conditions, which confirm the circulation of spin-waves over several loops around the particle. This work demonstrates the possibility to steer spin-waves onto a circular path using inhomogeneous magnetic landscape, as well as advancing scalable spin-wave-based information processing technologies.

title: Orbital-angular-momentum control of localized Floquet states and photocurrents in Weyl semimetals
summary: Structured light provides a route to controlling quantum materials not only through its polarization, but also through its spatial profile and orbital angular momentum (OAM). We develop real space theories of a Weyl semimetal driven by a vortex beam and show that optical OAM generates highly localized Floquet vortex states with pronounced circulating photocurrents. Exploiting cylindrical symmetry, we derive a Bogoliubov-de Gennes-like radial equation that resolves the states by angular momentum and reveals their evolution between the light-dressed Weyl cones. For Laguerre-Gaussian beams, the spatially varying drive produces strong hybridization between localized vortex states and bulk states. We complement this continuum description with a Wilson-lattice formulation that retains the full two-dimensional spatial structure and enables direct calculation of local photocurrents. Both approaches consistently identify OAM-induced vortex states localized around the beam axis. The lattice calculation further shows that these states support substantially stronger circulating current densities than the more extended surface states, with the largest current densities associated with the most strongly localized, low-angular-momentum vortex modes. Our results establish optical OAM as a tunable control parameter for creating and manipulating localized current-carrying states in Weyl systems and provide a real-space framework for studying photocurrents generated by spatially structured light.

title: Quantum Formulation of the Spinterface Model
summary: We present a fully quantum formulation of the spinterface model for the chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) effect, implemented within the non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism. The model consists of a gold atom hosting a localised magnetic moment, coupled to a chiral molecular chain with Rashba spin-orbit coupling, and contacted by two non-magnetic leads. The magnetic moment is determined self-consistently from the non-equilibrium electronic distribution, and the spin-resolved transmission is computed from the mean-field Hamiltonian. We show that the interfacial magnetic moment and the chiral Rashba term cooperate to produce large current polarisations that reproduce the key experimental signatures of CISS: high polarisation, a threshold emergence at four total sites followed by interference-modulated growth with chain length, thermal suppression, and sign reversal upon chirality inversion. The central new result of this work is a clean separation of the CISS effect into an even (achiral) and an odd (chiral) contribution to the spin current, $I_{S_z}(φ) = I_{S_z}^{\rm even}(φ) + I_{S_z}^{\rm odd}(φ)$. We demonstrate that $I_{S_z}^{\rm odd}$ vanishes exactly at fixed $m_z$ for chains of fewer than four sites and becomes non-zero for chains of four or more sites, with the smallest junction exhibiting a non-zero odd part being the four-site geometry (one gold atom plus three molecular sites). The odd part arises from reciprocity breaking in a device that is simultaneously chiral, magnetically asymmetric (moment on the gold end only), and long enough to support two or more Rashba-active bonds. This provides a direct, parameter-free test of whether an observed spin signal is genuinely chiral or arises from an achiral spin-valve mechanism.

title: Grain-Boundary Scattering between Chiral Domains in Chiral Topological Semimetal CoSi
summary: We evaluate the electron scattering properties in CoSi thin films having either twin (heterochiral) or non-twin (homochiral) grain boundaries using first-principles quantum transport calculations. We find that scattering across a twin grain boundary is more resistive than scattering across a non-twin grain boundary and that non-twin grain boundaries have a greater percentage of surface conduction than twin grain boundaries. This is corroborated by the transmission eigenstate profiles, which show that the surface Fermi-arc electrons can transmit past the non-twin grain boundaries between homochiral domains on the same surface without significant backscattering. In contrast, these surface electrons get scattered along the twin grain boundaries between heterochiral domains to the opposite surface, resulting in partial forward transmission and partial backscattering that yields higher grain-boundary resistivity. This work helps elucidate the complexities of electron transport in chiral topological semimetals for potential application in next-generation nano-interconnects.

title: Vortex matter as a magnetically programmable metasurface for tuning near-field radiative heat transfer
summary: Near-field radiative heat transfer (NFRHT) is of great interest for energy conversion and thermal management. Recent work on NFRHT has shown that metasurfaces can enhance NFRHT and reshape its spectral characteristics. Here, we show that the vortex lattice of a type-II superconductor represents a self-assembled metasurface whose lattice dimensions, in contrast to most other metasurfaces, can be tuned by magnetic fields, allowing NFRHT to be varied by orders of magnitude. Specifically, we show that for two Nb surfaces at 4.2 K and separated by a 100 nm gap, NFRHT can be magnetically tuned by a factor >200. Further, we show that the tuning range grows upon cooling, exceeding 10^5 at 2 K, which is far beyond the order-unity modulation of many proposed schemes for tuning NFRHT. Our results establish vortex matter as a magnetically programmable thermal metasurface and open new opportunities for tuning the flow of heat at the nanoscale.
